ENCOUNTER NOTE
Date: 2022-01-15
Provider: Dr. James Wilson, MD
Department: Rheumatology
Visit Type: outpatient

CHIEF COMPLAINT:
Persistent fevers and joint pain for the past 7 weeks

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
This 9-year-old female with complex medical history returns to Rheumatology for persistent fevers and joint pain following similar assessment in Dermatology six months prior. The fevers occur daily, typically in the late afternoon, and are accompanied by a transient pink rash on her trunk and extremities. Her parents report she has been increasingly fatigued and has had a decreased appetite.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
Active Problem List:
- Nutritional rickets (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Celiac disease (diagnosed 2020-07-15)
- Sturge-Weber syndrome (intracranial vascular malformation) (diagnosed 2021-01-15)
- Polyarticular JIA pattern (diagnosed 2021-07-15)
- Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
- Sickle Cell Trait
- Mild Intermittent Asthma
- Systemic Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis
- Sturge-Weber Syndrome
- Vitamin D Deficiency Rickets

She is up-to-date on all vaccinations.

MEDICATIONS:
Home Medications:
- Insulin glargine 8 units subcutaneous at bedtime
- Insulin lispro per carbohydrate ratio with meals
- Albuterol 90 mcg inhaler, 2 puffs every 4 hours as needed for wheezing
- Ibuprofen 200 mg orally every 6 hours as needed for joint pain
- Cholecalciferol (Vitamin D3) 2000 IU orally daily
- Calcium carbonate 500 mg orally twice daily

ALLERGIES:
No known drug allergies

FAMILY HISTORY:
- Father with Sickle Cell Trait
- Maternal grandmother with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
- Paternal uncle with Celiac Disease
- Mother with Autoimmune Hypothyroidism

SOCIAL HISTORY:
Smoking: Never. Alcohol: Never. Occupation: Student.

VITAL SIGNS:
Temperature of 39.2°C (102.5°F)

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
On physical examination, the patient has noticeable swelling and tenderness of her knees and wrists. Additionally, the pediatrician notes mild hepatosplenomegaly and a few enlarged, non-tender cervical lymph nodes.

LABORATORY DATA:
Laboratory tests reveal the following:

- Hemoglobin: 10.2 g/dL (normal: 11.5-15.5 g/dL)
- White blood cell count: 18,000/mm³ (normal: 4,500-11,000/mm³)
- Platelet count: 450,000/mm³ (normal: 150,000-400,000/mm³)
- Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 70 mm/hr (normal: 0-20 mm/hr)
- C-reactive protein (CRP): 4.5 mg/dL (normal: <0.8 mg/dL)
- Ferritin: 3000 ng/mL (normal: 15-200 ng/mL)

ENCOUNTER NOTE
Date: 2021-01-15
Provider: Dr. Michael O'Brien, MD
Department: Gastroenterology
Visit Type: outpatient

CHIEF COMPLAINT:
Blood in stool

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient is an 8-year-old female with a known history of Celiac Disease, Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus, and Sturge-Weber Syndrome who returns to the Gastroenterology clinic for further evaluation. She was last seen in this department six months prior for concerns regarding poor growth and persistent abdominal pain, and continues to receive multidisciplinary care for her complex medical conditions. The parents report that approximately three weeks ago, they began to notice streaks of bright red blood on the surface of her stool. Initially they attributed this to constipation, though the child has continued to have normal, well-formed bowel movements without straining. Over the past two weeks, her mother has observed that the patient has become increasingly fatigued with decreased energy during play. Her teachers have also commented that she often appears pale compared to her classmates. The patient has complained intermittently of abdominal pain, sometimes localizing to the periumbilical region. Her appetite has decreased slightly, and she frequently refuses to finish meals. Upon further questioning, the parents note that several dark spots on her lips have been present since she was a toddler; these spots have persisted over the years and have become slightly darker. They initially believed these were freckles, but have also observed similar spots on the inside of her cheeks.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
Active Problem List:
- Nutritional rickets (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Celiac disease (diagnosed 2020-07-15)
- Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
- Sickle Cell Trait
- Mild Intermittent Asthma
- Systemic Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis
- Sturge-Weber Syndrome
- Vitamin D Deficiency Rickets

MEDICATIONS:
Home Medications:
- Insulin glargine 8 units subcutaneous at bedtime
- Insulin lispro per carbohydrate ratio with meals
- Albuterol 90 mcg inhaler, 2 puffs every 4 hours as needed for wheezing
- Ibuprofen 200 mg orally every 6 hours as needed for joint pain
- Cholecalciferol (Vitamin D3) 2000 IU orally daily
- Calcium carbonate 500 mg orally twice daily

ALLERGIES:
No known drug allergies

FAMILY HISTORY:
Her father also has similar pigmented lesions on his lips and oral mucosa. The father recalls undergoing multiple colonoscopies in his 20s and 30s for removal of intestinal polyps. A paternal aunt was diagnosed with breast cancer in her late 30s. The paternal grandfather died of pancreatic cancer in his 50s. The mother’s family history is unremarkable. No other siblings are affected. The family is concerned that the daughter may have inherited a condition that “runs in the family.”

SOCIAL HISTORY:
Smoking: Never. Alcohol: Never. Occupation: Student.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS:
There has been no nausea or vomiting. There has been no recent fever, cough, or upper respiratory illness.

VITAL SIGNS:
Her vital signs are within normal limits.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
On physical examination, the child appears slightly underweight for her age. Her weight is at the 20th percentile, whereas it was previously closer to the 50th percentile a year ago. Her conjunctivae appear pale. Oral examination reveals multiple 2- to 3-mm pigmented macules on the buccal mucosa and on the vermillion border of the lips. There are no ulcers or vesicles. Her abdomen is soft, with mild tenderness in the periumbilical region. There is no rebound or guarding. There are no palpable masses. There is no hepatosplenomegaly. Rectal examination reveals normal sphincter tone and no masses. The stool sample is guaiac-positive.

LABORATORY DATA:
Laboratory testing shows hemoglobin of 9.0 g/dL, hematocrit of 27%, and mean corpuscular volume of 71 μm³. Leukocyte and platelet counts are normal. Iron studies are consistent with iron deficiency anemia.

IMAGING:
An abdominal ultrasound is unremarkable.

OTHER STUDIES:
The patient undergoes colonoscopy for further evaluation. The procedure reveals multiple pedunculated polyps scattered throughout the colon. Several similar polyps are visualized in the distal small intestine. The largest polyp measures 1.3 cm. Three polyps are removed for histopathology.

PLAN:
The parents are referred to genetic counseling for confirmation and family screening. The child is started on iron supplementation for anemia. A follow-up plan is arranged with pediatric gastroenterology and oncology.

ENCOUNTER NOTE
Date: 2022-07-15
Provider: Dr. James Wilson, MD
Department: Rheumatology
Visit Type: outpatient

CHIEF COMPLAINT:
Recurrent fevers and a rash for the past three weeks

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient is a 9-year-old female with systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis returning to rheumatology clinic with recurrent fevers and rash following evaluation six months ago for similar symptoms. The fevers occur daily, typically in the late afternoon, and are accompanied by a pink macular rash that appears on her trunk and proximal extremities. Her parents also report that she has been complaining of pain and stiffness in her knees and wrists for the last two months, which seems to be worse in the morning.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
Active Problem List:
- Nutritional rickets (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Celiac disease (diagnosed 2020-07-15)
- Sturge-Weber syndrome (intracranial vascular malformation) (diagnosed 2021-01-15)
- Polyarticular JIA pattern (diagnosed 2021-07-15)
- Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (diagnosed 2022-01-15)
- Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
- Sickle Cell Trait
- Mild Intermittent Asthma
- Sturge-Weber Syndrome
- Vitamin D Deficiency Rickets

The patient has a past medical history of mild intermittent asthma.

MEDICATIONS:
Home Medications:
- Insulin glargine 8 units subcutaneous at bedtime
- Insulin lispro per carbohydrate ratio with meals
- Albuterol 90 mcg inhaler, 2 puffs every 4 hours as needed for wheezing
- Ibuprofen 200 mg orally every 6 hours as needed for joint pain
- Cholecalciferol (Vitamin D3) 2000 IU orally daily
- Calcium carbonate 500 mg orally twice daily

ALLERGIES:
No known drug allergies

FAMILY HISTORY:
- Father with Sickle Cell Trait
- Maternal grandmother with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
- Paternal uncle with Celiac Disease
- Mother with Autoimmune Hypothyroidism

SOCIAL HISTORY:
Smoking: Never. Alcohol: Never. Occupation: Student.

VITAL SIGNS:
On physical examination, the patient has a temperature of 39.2°C (102.5°F), heart rate of 110/min

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
She is noted to have swollen and tender wrists and knees.

LABORATORY DATA:
A complete blood count and inflammatory markers are ordered, revealing the following:

- White blood cell count: 18,000/mm³ (Normal: 4,500-11,000/mm³)
- Hemoglobin: 9.8 g/dL (Normal: 11.5-15.5 g/dL)
- Platelet count: 550,000/mm³ (Normal: 150,000-400,000/mm³)
- Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 70 mm/hr (Normal: 0-20 mm/hr)
- C-reactive protein (CRP): 6.0 mg/dL (Normal: <0.8 mg/dL)

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
Based on the clinical presentation and laboratory findings,

ENCOUNTER NOTE
Date: 2023-01-15
Provider: Dr. Aisha Johnson, MD
Department: Hematology and Oncology
Visit Type: outpatient

CHIEF COMPLAINT:
Ongoing joint symptoms and persistent fatigue

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient is a 10-year-old female with established systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, celiac disease, and nutritional rickets who presents to the hematology clinic for ongoing evaluation of joint symptoms and persistent fatigue. She has been followed longitudinally in rheumatology for recurrent fevers and arthralgias, with her most recent rheumatology evaluation approximately six months prior for similar concerns. Her parents report that she has had multiple episodes over the past 4 months of joint pain and stiffness, especially in the knees, wrists, and ankles. The joint pain is worse in the mornings and often causes difficulty getting out of bed or walking to school. They have also noticed that her energy levels are lower than those of her peers and that she takes frequent naps after school. She occasionally develops a pink, patchy rash on her chest and abdomen that seems to worsen with fever and fades spontaneously. The rash is non-pruritic and does not leave marks. She has no known allergies, recent infections, or sick contacts. Her appetite has declined, and her weight is below the 10th percentile for her age.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
Active Problem List:
- Nutritional rickets (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Celiac disease (diagnosed 2020-07-15)
- Sturge-Weber syndrome (intracranial vascular malformation) (diagnosed 2021-01-15)

- Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (diagnosed 2022-01-15)
- Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
- Sickle Cell Trait
- Mild Intermittent Asthma
- Sturge-Weber Syndrome
- Vitamin D Deficiency Rickets

- Insulin glargine 8 units subcutaneous at bedtime
- Insulin lispro per carbohydrate ratio with meals
- Albuterol 90 mcg inhaler, 2 puffs every 4 hours as needed for wheezing
- Ibuprofen 200 mg orally every 6 hours as needed for joint pain
- Cholecalciferol (Vitamin D3) 2000 IU orally daily
- Calcium carbonate 500 mg orally twice daily

ALLERGIES:
No known allergies

FAMILY HISTORY:
- Father with Sickle Cell Trait
- Maternal grandmother with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
- Paternal uncle with Celiac Disease
- Mother with Autoimmune Hypothyroidism

SOCIAL HISTORY:
She has not traveled recently and is up to date on her vaccinations.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
On examination, she has mild swelling and limited range of motion in her wrists and both knees. A soft systolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border. Her spleen tip is palpable.

ENCOUNTER NOTE
Date: 2021-07-15
Provider: Dr. Priya Patel, MD
Department: Dermatology
Visit Type: outpatient

CHIEF COMPLAINT:
Recurrent episodes of fever and joint pain

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
This 8-year-old female with a history of systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, celiac disease, and Sturge-Weber syndrome, previously evaluated for nutritional rickets, chronic abdominal pain, and gastrointestinal bleeding, presents with recurrent episodes of fever and joint pain. Her parents report that over the past month she has had daily high fevers, usually peaking in the late afternoon or evening, that resolve spontaneously by the next morning. These fevers are often accompanied by a pink, blotchy rash on her trunk and upper limbs that appears and disappears with the fever spikes. The rash is non-pruritic and does not leave marks. She also complains of joint pain in her knees and wrists that worsens in the morning and improves throughout the day. She has become more fatigued and has missed several days of school.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
Active Problem List:
- Nutritional rickets (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Celiac disease (diagnosed 2020-07-15)
- Sturge-Weber syndrome (intracranial vascular malformation) (diagnosed 2021-01-15)
- Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
- Sickle Cell Trait
- Mild Intermittent Asthma
- Systemic Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis
- Sturge-Weber Syndrome
- Vitamin D Deficiency Rickets

MEDICATIONS:
Home Medications:
- Insulin glargine 8 units subcutaneous at bedtime
- Insulin lispro per carbohydrate ratio with meals
- Albuterol 90 mcg inhaler, 2 puffs every 4 hours as needed for wheezing
- Ibuprofen 200 mg orally every 6 hours as needed for joint pain
- Cholecalciferol (Vitamin D3) 2000 IU orally daily
- Calcium carbonate 500 mg orally twice daily

ALLERGIES:
No known drug allergies

FAMILY HISTORY:
- Father with Sickle Cell Trait
- Maternal grandmother with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
- Paternal uncle with Celiac Disease
- Mother with Autoimmune Hypothyroidism

SOCIAL HISTORY:
Smoking: Never. Alcohol: Never. Occupation: Student.

VITAL SIGNS:
On physical exam, her temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F).

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
There is visible swelling in both wrists and right knee with decreased range of motion, but no redness or warmth. The rest of her exam is normal.

LABORATORY DATA:
Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 10.2 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume of 82 fL, serum ferritin within normal limits, and low serum iron and transferrin. White blood cell count is mildly elevated and ESR is markedly elevated.
